## Code Status

Runs end to end. Last rendered 2026-11-16 with no errors (see the `.html` beside this file).
Feeds Section 7.8 of the capstone write-up (robustness of the method comparison).

## Purpose

1.  **Nested k-fold estimates** for the methods that choose tones from sample
    means (mean-only, top two, top three, ...), so no method is scored on the
    respondents used to choose its tones or its configuration.
2.  **How reliable is a person's tone profile?** If a respondent's best and
    worst tones do not repeat across contexts, any metric built on them is
    mostly noise. This section also brackets the true headroom.
3.  **Held-out optimization and disadvantage rates**, where a person's best and
    worst tones are labelled from two risk contexts and helpfulness is scored
    on the third.

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: Setup
# Load packages and this study's functions, then read the cleaned panel in long format
# (one row per message rating). The seed makes the cross-validation folds and bootstrap
# resamples repeatable.
options(conflicts.policy = "depends.ok")
library(tidyverse)

source("https://github.com/jjcurtin/lab_support/blob/main/format_path.R?raw=true")
source(here::here("scripts", "functions_llmpanel.R"))
source(here::here("scripts", "functions_assignment.R"))

path_processed <- format_path("llmpanel/data_processed")

panel_long <- format_eda(read_csv(
  here::here(path_processed, "panel.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE), long = TRUE)

# tone_levels and pref_cols are defined in functions_llmpanel.R

set.seed(102030)
```

*Settings*

```{r}
#| label: Settings
# Which messages to score on. "both" pools styles (6 messages per tone, 2 per
# context-by-tone cell) and is the default, since style changed tone ratings only
# slightly. "informal" uses only the messages that would be delivered (3 per tone)
# and was the setting for the first render (2026-11-16).
# Set in the YAML `params`. To render the other setting without editing the file:
#   quarto render heldout_methods.qmd -P styles_use:informal -o heldout_methods_informal.html
# Interactively, `params` is not defined, so the default below is used.
styles_use <- if (exists("params")) params$styles_use else "both"   # "informal" or "both"

# Cross-validation structure (matches the model: inner 2 x 5, outer 6 x 5)
outer_repeats <- 6
outer_folds <- 5
inner_repeats <- 2
inner_folds <- 5

# Selection rule: among configurations whose inner-loop mean helpfulness is
# within `tolerance` points of the best one, choose the one with the most variety.
tolerance <- 0.05

n_boot <- 2000
```

*Respondent-level data*

```{r}
#| label: Data
ratings_use <- if (styles_use == "informal") {
  panel_long |> filter(style == "informal")
} else {
  panel_long
}

# Respondent mean rating per tone, and the same as a respondent x tone matrix
tone_means <- ratings_use |>
  summarise(rating = mean(rating_num, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(subid, tone))

rating_wide <- tone_means |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = tone, values_from = rating) |>
  arrange(subid) |>
  drop_na()
M <- as.matrix(rating_wide[, tone_levels])
ids <- rating_wide$subid
n <- nrow(M)

# Respondent mean rating per context and tone (for Sections 2 and 3)
context_means <- ratings_use |>
  summarise(rating = mean(rating_num, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(subid, context, tone))

# Preference score per respondent and tone
pref_by_tone <- panel_long |>
  distinct(subid, across(all_of(pref_cols))) |>
  pivot_longer(-subid, names_to = "tone", names_prefix = "pref_", values_to = "pref")

dim(M)
```

# 1. Nested K-Fold Estimates

## Configurations

Each configuration turns a ranking of tones (best first, from training
respondents only) into a set of weights. `variety` is the effective number of
tones a person sees, 1 / sum(weight^2): 1 for a single tone, 5 for an even
five-tone rotation.

```{r}
#| label: Configurations
configs <- list(
  "Mean-only"                = \(top) set_names(1, top[1]),
  "Top two, 60/40"           = \(top) set_names(c(.6, .4), top[1:2]),
  "Top two, equal"           = \(top) set_names(c(.5, .5), top[1:2]),
  "Top three, 45/45/10"      = \(top) set_names(c(.45, .45, .10), top[1:3]),
  "Top three, 40/40/20"      = \(top) set_names(c(.40, .40, .20), top[1:3]),
  "Top three, equal"         = \(top) set_names(rep(1 / 3, 3), top[1:3]),
  "Top four, equal"          = \(top) set_names(rep(1 / 4, 4), top[1:4]),
  "All five, 30/30/20/10/10" = \(top) set_names(c(.3, .3, .2, .1, .1), top[1:5]),
  "Uniform (all five)"       = \(top) set_names(rep(1 / 5, 5), top[1:5]))

config_variety <- map_dbl(configs, \(f) 1 / sum(f(tone_levels)^2))
config_variety
```

*Helpers*

```{r}
#| label: CV Helpers
# Tones ranked by mean rating among the given respondents (row numbers of M)
rank_tones <- function(rows) {
  names(sort(colMeans(M[rows, , drop = FALSE]), decreasing = TRUE))
}

# Each respondent's expected rating under a weight vector
method_value <- function(rows, w) {
  as.numeric(M[rows, names(w), drop = FALSE] %*% w)
}

# Folds come from make_folds() in functions_assignment.R: repeated k-fold, each fold a
# list(rep, fold, test) with the held-out rows

# Mean helpfulness of every configuration, tones ranked on `fit`, scored on `val`
score_configs <- function(fit, val) {
  top <- rank_tones(fit)
  map_dbl(configs, \(f) mean(method_value(val, f(top))))
}

# Choose a configuration from inner-loop means
#   "best":      highest mean
#   "tolerance": most variety among those within `tolerance` of the highest mean
select_config <- function(inner_means, rule = c("best", "tolerance")) {
  rule <- match.arg(rule)
  if (rule == "best") return(names(which.max(inner_means)))
  ok <- names(inner_means)[inner_means >= max(inner_means) - tolerance]
  ok[which.max(config_variety[ok])]
}
```

## Nested Loop

For each outer split:

1.  Rank tones on the outer training respondents and score **every fixed
    configuration** on the outer test respondents. This is the honest estimate
    for each method on its own.
2.  Run the inner loop on the outer training respondents only, to **select a
    configuration** by each rule. Re-rank tones on the full outer training
    set, then score the selected configuration on the outer test respondents.
    This is the honest estimate for "pick the best method, then use it".

```{r}
#| label: Nested CV
outer <- make_folds(seq_len(n), outer_folds, outer_repeats)

nested <- map(outer, \(o) {
  test <- o$test
  train <- setdiff(seq_len(n), test)
  top_train <- rank_tones(train)

  # 1. Every fixed configuration on the outer test set
  fixed <- imap(configs, \(f, nm) {
    tibble(method = nm, row = test, rating = method_value(test, f(top_train)))
  }) |> list_rbind()

  # 2. Inner loop: mean helpfulness of each configuration on validation folds
  inner <- make_folds(train, inner_folds, inner_repeats)
  inner_means <- map(inner, \(i) score_configs(setdiff(train, i$test), i$test)) |>
    do.call(what = rbind) |>
    colMeans()

  chosen_best <- select_config(inner_means, "best")
  chosen_tol <- select_config(inner_means, "tolerance")

  selected <- bind_rows(
    tibble(method = "Selected: highest mean", row = test,
           rating = method_value(test, configs[[chosen_best]](top_train))),
    tibble(method = paste0("Selected: most variety within ", tolerance), row = test,
           rating = method_value(test, configs[[chosen_tol]](top_train))))

  list(
    ratings = bind_rows(fixed, selected) |> mutate(rep = o$rep, fold = o$fold),
    choice = tibble(rep = o$rep, fold = o$fold, top_tone = top_train[1],
                    top_three = paste(sort(top_train[1:3]), collapse = " + "),
                    chosen_best = chosen_best, chosen_tol = chosen_tol))
})

nested_ratings <- map(nested, "ratings") |> list_rbind() |> mutate(subid = ids[row])
nested_choice <- map(nested, "choice") |> list_rbind()
```

## What Was Chosen

```{r}
#| label: Choices
# Stability of the tone ranking across outer training sets
nested_choice |> count(top_tone)
nested_choice |> count(top_three)

# Which configuration each rule selected
nested_choice |> count(chosen_best, sort = TRUE)
nested_choice |> count(chosen_tol, sort = TRUE)
```

## Held-Out Performance

Fold-level summary: mean and SD of the 30 outer test-set means.

```{r}
#| label: Fold Summary
method_order <- c(names(configs), "Selected: highest mean",
                  paste0("Selected: most variety within ", tolerance))

fold_summary <- nested_ratings |>
  summarise(fold_mean = mean(rating), .by = c(method, rep, fold)) |>
  summarise(held_out = mean(fold_mean), sd_across_folds = sd(fold_mean), .by = method)

# In-sample value: tones ranked on the full sample and scored on the full sample
in_sample <- score_configs(seq_len(n), seq_len(n))

fold_summary |>
  left_join(enframe(in_sample, "method", "in_sample"), by = "method") |>
  left_join(enframe(config_variety, "method", "variety"), by = "method") |>
  mutate(optimism = in_sample - held_out,
         method = factor(method, levels = method_order)) |>
  arrange(method)
```

Respondent-level summary: each respondent is in a test set once per repeat, so
their held-out rating under each method is averaged over the 6 repeats. The
bootstrap then gives paired intervals against held-out mean-only. The two
preference-based methods are added for comparison. They do not choose tones
from the sample, so they need no cross-validation.

```{r}
#| label: Respondent Summary
heldout_wide <- nested_ratings |>
  summarise(rating = mean(rating), .by = c(subid, method)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = rating)

# Preference-based methods (fixed rules, scored directly)
pref_methods <- list(
  "Drop own two least-preferred" = drop_least_preferred(pref_by_tone, n_drop = 2) |>
    mutate(weight = 1),
  "Rule-based" = data_driven_weights(pref_by_tone) |> select(subid, tone, weight))

pref_wide <- imap(pref_methods, \(w, nm) {
  weighted_method(w, label = nm, tone_ratings = tone_means) |>
    transmute(subid, method = nm, rating = weighted_rating)
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = rating)

compare_wide <- heldout_wide |>
  inner_join(pref_wide, by = "subid") |>
  drop_na()
compare_mat <- as.matrix(select(compare_wide, -subid))
reference <- "Mean-only"

boot_means <- map(seq_len(n_boot), \(i) {
  colMeans(compare_mat[sample(nrow(compare_mat), replace = TRUE), , drop = FALSE])
}) |>
  do.call(what = rbind)

heldout_summary <- tibble(
  method = colnames(compare_mat),
  mean = colMeans(compare_mat),
  mean_low = apply(boot_means, 2, quantile, .025),
  mean_high = apply(boot_means, 2, quantile, .975),
  diff_vs_ref = colMeans(compare_mat) - mean(compare_mat[, reference]),
  diff_low = apply(boot_means - boot_means[, reference], 2, quantile, .025),
  diff_high = apply(boot_means - boot_means[, reference], 2, quantile, .975)) |>
  arrange(mean)
heldout_summary
```

```{r}
#| label: Held-Out Plot
# Forest plot: each method's held-out mean difference from the reference method, with
# its 95% bootstrap interval
heldout_summary |>
  filter(method != reference) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = diff_vs_ref, y = fct_reorder(method, diff_vs_ref))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = diff_low, xmax = diff_high)) +
  labs(x = paste0("Held-out difference in mean helpfulness vs. ", reference,
                  " (95% bootstrap interval)"),
       y = NULL)
```

Reading the results:

-   `optimism` near zero means the full-sample figure was already fair.
    Expect it to be largest for mean-only, which has the most to lose from
    picking the wrong tone.
-   The "Selected" rows are the figures to quote if the paper describes a
    procedure ("choose the configuration, then deploy it") and not one fixed
    method.
-   The bootstrap resamples respondents but not the fold assignment, so the
    intervals are slightly narrow. The SD across folds above is the check.

# 2. How Reliable Is a Person's Tone Profile?

A person's "best" and "worst" tones only mean something if their tone profile
repeats. Here each respondent's profile (their rating of each tone relative to
their own average) is compared across the three risk contexts.

## Profile Reliability

Two versions of each person's profile:

-   **Total:** tone rating minus the person's mean in that context. Includes
    the tone order everyone shares.
-   **Individual-specific:** additionally minus the sample's mean for that
    tone in that context. What is left is the person's own taste.

The correlation between contexts is the reliability of a single context's
profile. Spearman-Brown projects it to the full three-context profile.

```{r}
#| label: Profile Reliability
profiles <- context_means |>
  mutate(total = rating - mean(rating), .by = c(subid, context)) |>
  mutate(individual = total - mean(total), .by = c(context, tone))

profile_wide <- profiles |>
  select(subid, tone, context, total, individual) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = context, values_from = c(total, individual))

contexts <- sort(unique(context_means$context))
context_pairs <- combn(contexts, 2, simplify = FALSE)

profile_reliability <- map(context_pairs, \(p) {
  tibble(
    pair = paste(p, collapse = " vs. "),
    r_total = cor(profile_wide[[paste0("total_", p[1])]],
                  profile_wide[[paste0("total_", p[2])]], use = "complete.obs"),
    r_individual = cor(profile_wide[[paste0("individual_", p[1])]],
                       profile_wide[[paste0("individual_", p[2])]], use = "complete.obs"))
}) |> list_rbind()
profile_reliability

spearman_brown <- \(r, k) k * r / (1 + (k - 1) * r)
profile_reliability |>
  summarise(across(starts_with("r_"), mean)) |>
  mutate(rel3_total = spearman_brown(r_total, 3),
         rel3_individual = spearman_brown(r_individual, 3))
```

`rel3_individual` is the share of the variance in people's individual tone
profiles (over all three contexts) that is real and not rating noise. Low
values mean best and worst tones are mostly luck.

## Do Best and Worst Tones Repeat?

For each respondent, the best tone(s) from two contexts are compared with the
best tone(s) in the third. "Agreement" is whether they share at least one
tone. The chance rate comes from shuffling tone labels within each respondent
in the held-out context.

```{r}
#| label: Label Agreement
labels_from <- function(d) {
  d |>
    summarise(rating = mean(rating), .by = c(subid, tone)) |>
    summarise(best = list(tone[near(rating, max(rating))]),
              worst = list(tone[near(rating, min(rating))]),
              .by = subid)
}

label_agreement <- map(contexts, \(held) {
  train_labels <- labels_from(filter(context_means, context != held))
  test <- filter(context_means, context == held)
  test_labels <- labels_from(test)
  # Chance: permute tone labels within respondent in the held-out context
  shuffled_labels <- test |>
    mutate(tone = sample(tone), .by = subid) |>
    labels_from()

  train_labels |>
    inner_join(test_labels, by = "subid", suffix = c("_train", "_test")) |>
    inner_join(shuffled_labels |> rename(best_shuf = best, worst_shuf = worst),
               by = "subid") |>
    summarise(
      held_out = held,
      best_agree = mean(map2_lgl(best_train, best_test, \(a, b) any(a %in% b))),
      best_chance = mean(map2_lgl(best_train, best_shuf, \(a, b) any(a %in% b))),
      worst_agree = mean(map2_lgl(worst_train, worst_test, \(a, b) any(a %in% b))),
      worst_chance = mean(map2_lgl(worst_train, worst_shuf, \(a, b) any(a %in% b))),
      # The reversal: labelled best turns out to be worst in the held-out context
      best_is_worst = mean(map2_lgl(best_train, worst_test, \(a, b) any(a %in% b))))
}) |> list_rbind()
label_agreement
```

Note: the chance rate here ignores the tone order everyone shares, so
agreement can beat it without any individual taste. Read it together with
`r_individual` above.

## Bracketing the True Headroom

Two estimates of how far an ideal assignment could beat the best single tone:

-   **Lower bound (achievable):** pick each person's best tone from two
    contexts, score it on the third. This is what a system could reach if it
    knew a handful of a person's ratings.
-   **Upper bound (oracle):** a mixed model separates stable person-by-tone
    differences from message noise. Simulating people from the fitted variance
    gives the helpfulness of each person's true best tone, which no realistic
    system could know exactly.

```{r}
#| label: Achievable Headroom
achievable <- map(contexts, \(held) {
  picked <- context_means |>
    filter(context != held) |>
    summarise(train_rating = mean(rating), .by = c(subid, tone)) |>
    mutate(is_best = near(train_rating, max(train_rating)),
           is_worst = near(train_rating, min(train_rating)),
           .by = subid)
  sample_top <- picked |>
    summarise(m = mean(train_rating), .by = tone) |>
    slice_max(m, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    pull(tone)

  picked |>
    inner_join(context_means |> filter(context == held) |>
                 select(subid, tone, test_rating = rating),
               by = c("subid", "tone")) |>
    summarise(best_case = mean(test_rating[is_best]),
              worst_case = mean(test_rating[is_worst]),
              uniform = mean(test_rating),
              mean_only = mean(test_rating[tone == sample_top]),
              .by = subid)
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  summarise(across(everything(), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)), .by = subid) |>
  summarise(across(-subid, \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)))
achievable
```

```{r}
#| label: Oracle Headroom
m_var <- lme4::lmer(
  rating_num ~ tone + context + (1 | subid) + (1 | subid:tone),
  data = ratings_use |> mutate(subid = factor(subid), tone = factor(tone)),
  REML = TRUE)
lme4::VarCorr(m_var)

sd_person_tone <- attr(lme4::VarCorr(m_var)[["subid:tone"]], "stddev")[[1]]
tone_mu <- colMeans(M)

# Simulate true tone values for many people: shared tone means plus a stable
# person-by-tone deviation. The person's overall level cancels out of every
# comparison, so it is left at zero.
n_sim <- 100000
true_values <- matrix(rnorm(n_sim * 5, mean = 0, sd = sd_person_tone), ncol = 5) +
  matrix(tone_mu, nrow = n_sim, ncol = 5, byrow = TRUE)

oracle <- tibble(
  sd_person_tone = sd_person_tone,
  worst_case = mean(apply(true_values, 1, min)),
  uniform = mean(tone_mu),
  mean_only = max(tone_mu),
  best_case = mean(apply(true_values, 1, max)))
oracle

# The bracket
tibble(
  estimate = c("In-sample (inflated by noise)", "Oracle (upper bound)",
               "Achievable from two contexts (lower bound)"),
  headroom_over_mean_only = c(
    mean(apply(M, 1, max)) - max(tone_mu),
    oracle$best_case - oracle$mean_only,
    achievable$best_case - achievable$mean_only))
```

The oracle figure assumes normal, independent person-by-tone deviations and
treats the estimated variance as exact. Treat it as a rough ceiling.

# 3. Held-Out Optimization and Disadvantage Rates

In `tone_assignment_methods.qmd` a person's best and worst tones come from the
same ratings used to score helpfulness. Here they are labelled from two risk
contexts, and helpfulness is scored on the third, so no rating is used for
both. Each context takes a turn as the held-out one.

For each method and held-out context:

-   `held_out_mean`: mean helpfulness in the held-out context.
-   `opt_rate` / `dis_rate`: average share of a person's messages in the
    tone(s) labelled best / worst from the other two contexts.
-   `regret`: honest best case (the labelled-best tone, scored held out) minus
    the method's held-out mean. Lower is better.

Tones for the data-chosen methods are ranked on the two labelling contexts.

```{r}
#| label: Held-Out Rates
fixed_weights <- function(tones, weights = rep(1 / length(tones), length(tones))) {
  expand_grid(subid = ids, tibble(tone = tones, weight = weights))
}

heldout_rates <- map(contexts, \(held) {
  train <- context_means |>
    filter(context != held) |>
    summarise(rating = mean(rating), .by = c(subid, tone))
  test <- context_means |>
    filter(context == held) |>
    select(subid, tone, test_rating = rating)

  top <- train |>
    summarise(m = mean(rating), .by = tone) |>
    arrange(desc(m)) |>
    pull(tone)

  labels <- train |>
    mutate(is_best = near(rating, max(rating)),
           is_worst = near(rating, min(rating)),
           .by = subid) |>
    select(subid, tone, is_best, is_worst)

  methods <- c(
    list("Uniform (all five)" = fixed_weights(tone_levels),
         "Top three, equal" = fixed_weights(top[1:3]),
         "Top three, 40/40/20" = fixed_weights(top[1:3], c(.4, .4, .2)),
         "Top two, equal" = fixed_weights(top[1:2]),
         "Mean-only" = fixed_weights(top[1])),
    map(pref_methods, \(w) mutate(w, weight = weight / sum(weight), .by = subid)))

  honest_best <- labels |>
    inner_join(test, by = c("subid", "tone")) |>
    summarise(best = mean(test_rating[is_best]), .by = subid) |>
    summarise(best = mean(best, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    pull(best)

  imap(methods, \(w, nm) {
    w |>
      inner_join(labels, by = c("subid", "tone")) |>
      inner_join(test, by = c("subid", "tone")) |>
      summarise(value = sum(weight * test_rating) / sum(weight),
                opt = sum(weight[is_best]) / sum(weight),
                dis = sum(weight[is_worst]) / sum(weight),
                .by = subid) |>
      summarise(method = nm, held_out = held,
                held_out_mean = mean(value),
                opt_rate = mean(opt),
                dis_rate = mean(dis),
                regret = honest_best - mean(value))
  }) |> list_rbind()
}) |> list_rbind()

# Averaged over the three held-out contexts
heldout_rates |>
  summarise(across(c(held_out_mean, opt_rate, dis_rate, regret), mean), .by = method) |>
  arrange(held_out_mean)

# By held-out context
heldout_rates |> arrange(held_out, held_out_mean)
```

How to read this against the in-sample rates:

-   If `rel3_individual` in Section 2 is low, the opt and dis rates mostly
    measure agreement with noisy labels, and differences between methods on
    those rates should not carry the argument. `held_out_mean` and `regret`
    are the safer headline numbers.
-   Rates here use labels from two contexts (fewer messages than the full
    sample), so they are noisier than the in-sample rates, not cleaner. Their
    value is that helpfulness and labels are never drawn from the same
    ratings.
